context: repetition-led · guest-room mock-up gates the typical-floor cycle; back-of-house plant drives the tail

brief.intro: New to this project type? A hotel is really two projects in one: a repetitive vertical stack of near-identical guest rooms (the "keys"), and a heavily serviced, one-off back-of-house and public-area podium — kitchens, laundry, pools, spa, ballroom, lobby. The guest-room programme is driven by a single mock-up room, built and approved early, that locks the finishes, MEP layout and joinery for every room on every typical floor; once it's approved, the typical-floor cycle repeats at a steady, predictable rate. The back-of-house, by contrast, is design-intensive, equipment-heavy and doesn't repeat, so it needs its own separate sequence and often becomes the tail of the programme rather than the guest towers.

must_get_right: Lock and approve the mock-up room early — every typical-floor activity (MEP, waterproofing, tiling, joinery) is copied from it, so a late mock-up delays the entire guest-tower programme.
Wet-area waterproofing and DHW quality are the classic hotel snag sources — build in proper cure/test time per floor, not just a walk-through.
Back-of-house and F&B areas are design-intensive and equipment-heavy, not repetitive — schedule and resource them separately from the typical-floor rollout, and don't assume they will "catch up".
Protect real time for brand/operator technical-services sign-off and FF&E installation before opening — these sit outside the base-build trades and are frequently underestimated.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Guest-room typical floors are tracked as a repetitive production line — rooms or floors completed per week — rather than as individually estimated activities.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and envelope run a 6-day week; once the mock-up is approved, the typical-floor MEP and finishing rollout runs on a fixed floor-cycle duration (one floor released to finishing every set number of days). Back-of-house and commissioning move to extended hours as opening approaches.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs mock-up room build & approval → typical-floor rollout (structure staying a few floors ahead of finishing) → back-of-house/F&B plant, which runs in parallel on its own critical path → DHW flushing → integrated life-safety test → operator technical-services sign-off → opening. Whichever finishes later — the typical-floor rollout or the back-of-house completion — governs the opening date.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Brand/operator technical standards are finalised before the mock-up is built; a single mobilisation; FF&E supply and installation are coordinated on a separate but interfacing programme; and no room-count or layout changes occur after mock-up approval.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is procurement-led for vertical transport, central plant and back-of-house equipment. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Before typical-floor handover to the FF&E installer

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Tower hoists and access are shared between structure and finishing trades; finishing-crew resourcing is sized to hold the floor-cycle rate. Back-of-house equipment deliveries need crane or loading-dock windows, and brand technical-services site visits occur at fixed programme gates that must be planned around.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: a late mock-up approval (which delays every typical floor), wet-area waterproofing failures or re-work, back-of-house design changes, and integrated life-safety re-test loops. Schedule contingency is held before the mock-up approval gate and before the integrated life-safety test/opening, rather than spread thinly across floors.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead per floor/zone for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
